newsitem.title: USA: N.J. proposes stricter natgas pipeline safety laws.
newsitem.headline: N.J. proposes stricter natgas pipeline safety laws.

text.p: New Jersey, home to about 378 miles of intrastate underground natural gas pipeline, took a big step this week toward implementing the strictest pipeline safety regulations in the country.

The Board of Public Utilities (BPU) on Tuesday approved a measure that would require natural gas companies to install remote control or automatic emergency shutoff valves at strategic points on their intrastate gas transmission lines.
The number of valves needed would be determined by population density along each line.
To ensure the law's effectiveness, each year the gas companies would be required to assess the valves and submit a written evaluation of their emergency closure plans.

The BPU's proposed ruling also calls for strictly enforcing internal inspections, monthly line patrols, public education, monitoring third party excavations, and better surface markings on underground transmission pipelines.
Many pipeline companies are already involved in these programs, but the proposed rule would make them mandatory.
The BPU said that since the One-Call law's inception, hits on underground facilities are down 17 percent.
There are currently about 378 miles of natural gas intrastate pipeline and 1,000 miles of interstate pipeline in densely populated New Jersey.
The BPU has jurisdiction over intrastate but not interstate lines.

New Jersey Natural Gas Co, which operates about 200 miles of the state's total intrastate pipeline system, has already installed safety valves on its newer pipelines and supports the BPU's efforts, company spokesman David Klucsik said.
However, he said, the rule "needs to be addressed on a system-by-system basis," noting risk management and engineering studies would be needed to determine where the valves would be required.
The proposed rule will be submitted for public comment and will likely be adopted in about three months, the BPU said.
